poems.title: The Man Who Fed the Pigeons
poemText: an old man in a grey coat
the way one knows church bells
and the pigeons came all the same
The clerk who had signed the sign
watched from the town hall window
on the third day he came down
What are you feeding them? he asked sternly
The bread, that was for you
so you'd have something to forbid
They never came here for bread

poster.style: Born litografie — centralni ramovana scena + siroka margie s marginaliemi, tlumena olive/ochre/sepia
poster.prompt:
Study the attached lithographs by Adolf Born and imitate their TECHNIQUE precisely — not their subjects. Reproduce: the granular lithographic stipple texture, the soft airbrushed color fields, the fine hatched line work, the whimsical elongated caricature figures, the aged warm paper, and the overall feel of a precious old print. Compose it as a central framed scene surrounded by a wide aged-paper margin decorated with small hand-drawn marginalia sketches and elegant calligraphic flourishes. Muted dusty palette of olive, ochre and sepia — restrained, antique.

Now the NEW subject, drawn in exactly that technique: an old man in a grey coat sits on a park bench like a living monument, entirely covered in adoring pigeons — pigeons on his shoulders, on his hat, on his knees, and on his wide-open, completely EMPTY hands. Next to the bench towers a comically oversized official prohibition board on a pole — a blank white board with a stern red diagonal stripe, no writing — and a tiny stiff clerk in a bowler hat gazes up at it, baffled that the pigeons ignore it. Behind them a small market square with a fountain. In the margins: a single breadcrumb, a lone falling feather, an official rubber stamp, a small church bell.

No text, no letters, no words anywhere. No signature, no edition number. Tender absurd humor, no kitsch. Portrait orientation 2:3.

poems.title: The Forgotten Umbrella
poemText: Mr. Novák bought himself an umbrella
so he would never get wet
he left it on the train to Brno
in Brno a student took it
and under it she kissed a boy
she was not supposed to kiss
and left it in a café
In the café a violinist took it
and played beneath it at the station
when rain fell on his sheet music
then he lent it to a bride
whose veil was catching the rain
and the bride left it in a taxi
and the taxi drove it all the way to the sea
And so the umbrella saw Brno
a kiss that wasn't allowed to be
Mr. Novák bought a new umbrella
and so as not to lose it again
because he was afraid of getting lost

poster.style: Born litografie — velka cista scena + spodni predella pruh, sytejsi barvy s akcentem vermilion/turquoise
poster.prompt:
Study the attached lithographs by Adolf Born and imitate their TECHNIQUE precisely — not their subjects. Reproduce: the granular lithographic stipple texture, the soft airbrushed color fields, the fine hatched line work, the whimsical elongated caricature figures, the aged warm paper, and the overall feel of a precious old print. Keep the scene large and clean, with one narrow horizontal strip of tiny predella scenes along the bottom edge only. Richer joyful saturated colors with one glowing accent of vermilion or turquoise.

Now the NEW subject, drawn in exactly that technique: one enormous open black umbrella sails majestically through the sky above the open sea like a proud ship under full wind, gulls escorting it, its curved handle trailing a ribbon of rain. Far below at the edge of the scene, tiny in his window, a cautious man in a buttoned coat clutches a brand-new umbrella indoors, watching the rain from behind glass, going nowhere. The predella strip along the bottom tells the lost umbrella's journey in tiny scenes: a railway carriage, a student kissing a boy beneath the umbrella, a violinist playing under it at a station, a bride sheltering her veil, a taxi driving toward the sea.

No text, no letters, no words anywhere. No signature, no edition number. Tender absurd humor, no kitsch. Portrait orientation 2:3.
